To travel is to become a wound that heals in unfamiliar light. You leave one self on the platform and arrive somewhere else wearing a thinner skin, the nerve endings newly exposed to the foreign air.

Cities speak in textures. Lisbon murmurs through crumbling azulejos and the metallic screech of ascending trams. Kyoto communicates in moss and the deliberate silence of raked gravel. Each place offers its own dialect of sensation... and the traveler must become fluent in bewilderment.

There is a particular loneliness that belongs exclusively to train stations at midnight. The fluorescent hum. The vendor closing his kiosk with the mechanical weariness of ritual. You stand between departures, belonging to neither the place you left nor the one approaching through the darkness.

But this displacement is the gift. Stripped of context, the self becomes porous, absorbent. You notice the weight of bread in an unfamiliar bakery. The angle of afternoon light falling across a courtyard becomes an event... a revelation wrapped in ordinariness.
